analysis.title: Wall Street Braces For Biggest Treasury Sales Overhaul In Years
key_insights: Dealers expect Treasury to change its quarterly refunding guidance on Wednesday, the biggest revamp since early 2024. A shift could pave the way for cuts in 2027 to sales of the longest-dated debt, balanced by larger bill and short-term note auctions.
Citigroup predicts Treasury will announce cuts to 20- and 30-year bond sales starting this month, which would effectively violate the guidance in the last refunding statement.

UBS (Phoebe White) says guidance is more likely than immediate action, and UBS sees no change in actual issuance until May. Treasury's recent unconventional behavior raises the odds that its actions deviate from historical precedent.

JPMorgan (Jay Barry) expects Treasury to keep the 'next several quarters' language into 2027 and hold auction sizes unchanged through next August. It then expects a series of increases focused on 2- to 10-year securities. JPMorgan says Treasury's 'discomfort with the level of yields' is at the heart of its recent actions.

Barclays (Anshul Pradhan) suggests replacing 'at least the next several quarters' with 'the coming quarters', which would give Treasury flexibility over the timing and composition of issuance. Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and UBS are also watching for a change.

The 30-year yield was above 5.30% on Friday, near mid-August levels when Bessent expanded buybacks. Longer-dated yields hit their highest in more than two decades in early October and have since retreated.

Heavier reliance on bills will eventually test investor appetite. The US now auctions more than half a trillion dollars of bills in a typical week, and sold a record $839 billion last week. The bill share of debt outstanding is about 22% as of September, above the 20% average TBAC advised in 2024.

JPMorgan argues cutting long bond sales would not be prudent given the borrowing required, and sees early signs that bill demand is stalling. Bill purchases by stablecoins have not materialized at scale.

Buybacks in the 10-year to 30-year sector were tripled to $6 billion each. Most investors expect that amount to stay, with the option to change. Goldman (William Marshall) says making buybacks an explicit part of the toolkit could strengthen the market impact and make Treasury less price sensitive.
If issuance sizes are unchanged, next week's refunding auctions total $125 billion: $58 billion 3-year on Nov. 9, $42 billion 10-year on Nov. 10, $25 billion 30-year on Nov. 12.

tension_points.bull_case: Citigroup expects cuts to 20- and 30-year bond sales starting this month. Barclays, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and UBS are watching for a change in the guidance language, which would give Treasury flexibility over timing and composition.
tension_points.bear_case: JPMorgan expects the 'next several quarters' language to stay into 2027 and auction sizes to stay unchanged through next August. It says cutting long bond sales is imprudent given borrowing needs and stalling bill demand.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Wednesday's refunding statement keeping the 'next several quarters' language would undercut the dealers expecting a change.
